extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Critical standards and practical guidance for evaluating and producing poetry—especially diction, style, and the relation of thought to poetic language, as argued by Coleridge in Biographia Literaria.

rubrics_metrics.name: fitness_of_word_choice_and_position
rubrics_metrics.description: In the truly great poets ... there is a reason assignable, not only for every word, but for the position of every word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words and their placement must be precisely fitted to purpose; Coleridge illustrates this by reference to classical practice (Didymus on Homer) and claims that altering a word or its position in great poetry (Milton, Shakespeare) typically makes the passage say something else or worse. Anti-pattern: careless synonym-replacement or reordering that leaves sense or effect unchanged or degraded.

rubrics_metrics.name: support_by_sound_sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrase, metaphor, or image unsupported by a sound sense, or where the same sense might be conveyed with equal force and dignity in plainer words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge’s schoolmaster punished unsupported figurative language; prefer metaphors and images that have real semantic grounding. Anti-patterns include decorative tropes used merely for ornament (e.g. 'harp', 'muse', 'Pegasus') with no substantive fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_clichés_and_stock_phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Banish ever-returning, well-known introductory and transitional phrases, modest egoisms, flattering illeisms, and other stock locutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge recommends an 'index expurgatorius' of trite poetic and rhetorical phrases (he gives Alexander and Clytus as an overused simile). Anti-pattern: recurring hackneyed examples or similes that appear in multiple contexts and lose aptness.

rubrics_metrics.name: internal_logic_and_coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry has a logic of its own, as severe as that of science: every sentence and placement should be accountable to the poem's internal reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional practice described: exercises were examined for whether sentences were in appropriate places; repeated faults led to rewriting. Evaluate poems for an internal necessity of structure, not mere ornament. Anti-pattern: passages that feel arbitrary or whose parts could be shuffled without harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: re-readability_as_mark_of_genuine_poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Not the poem which we have read, but that to which we return, with the greatest pleasure, possesses the genuine power, and claims the name of essential poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine poetry yields durable pleasure on repeated readings; transient effects (novelty, clever surprises) are insufficient. Scoring guidance: reward sustained pleasures and penalties for works that impress only once.

rubrics_metrics.name: non-translatability_of_diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever lines can be translated into other words of the same language, without diminution of their significance, either in sense or association, or in any worthy feeling, are so far vicious in their diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetic diction resists paraphrase—meaning and feeling are bound to specific phrasing. Anti-pattern: 'prose thoughts translated into poetic language'—lines that survive literal paraphrase without loss are judged weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: clarity_and_austerity_over_turgidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid obscurity, a general turgidness of diction, and a profusion of newly-coined double epithets; prefer an austere, more natural style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge admits early faults (obscurity, turgid diction, double epithets) and describes pruning them in later editions. Evaluate for clarity of thought and economy of ornament; penalize unnecessary coinages and swollen phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_excessive_ornament_and_strained_diction
rubrics_metrics.description: An excess of ornament, strained and elaborate diction, and profuse ornamentation are defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune ornamental matter that does not serve thought; Coleridge recounts deliberately removing such ornament even at cost to some lines. Anti-pattern: language that calls attention to cleverness rather than expressive necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: naturalness_of_language
rubrics_metrics.description: The preference for a manly simplicity and natural diction—language should be neither bookish nor vulgar, neither 'redolent of the lamp' nor 'of the kennel'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction for naturalness: neither artificially learned nor low/commonplace. Examples of good models: Cowper, Bowles, and elder English poets from Chaucer to Milton (in different ways).

rubrics_metrics.name: balance_of_heart_and_head
rubrics_metrics.description: The best poetry reconciles the heart with the head—combining natural thoughts with natural diction and uniting feeling and intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge praises poets who combine emotion and intellect; penalize works that sacrifice passion to wit or vice versa (e.g., elder poets sacrificing passion to subtleties of intellect; moderns sacrificing both to point and drapery).

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_affected_simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid low, creeping language presented under the pretence of simplicity (affected simplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of Coleridge’s three satirized sins: language pretended to be plain but actually impoverished. Anti-pattern: 'simplicity' that is mere vulgarity or laziness.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_indiscriminate_swollen_imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the indiscriminate use of elaborate, swelling language and heterogeneous imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another of the three sins: indiscriminate ornament and fantastical imagery that obscures genuine feeling. Penalize mixed, glittering image assemblages that have no organic relation to thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_novelty_for_its_own_sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude from worthy feeling the pleasure derived from mere novelty in the reader and the desire of exciting wonderment at the author’s powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine poetic admiration is an everywhere-present undercurrent, not a succession of novelty-induced exclamations. Anti-pattern: stylistic excesses designed only to astonish.

rubrics_metrics.name: preference_for_continuous_flow_over_epigrammatic_couplets
rubrics_metrics.description: Defend lines running into each other (enjambment) rather than closing each couplet with a point; oppose the doctrine that every point must come at the end of a couplet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge argues against the modern practice of expecting an epigrammatic point at every couplet (as in Pope). Reward rhythmic continuity and organic pacing rather than artificial couplet-closing points.

rubrics_metrics.name: suitability_of_subject_to_poetic_medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid giving a poetic colouring to abstract and metaphysical truths that require a degree of attention unsuitable to the nature and objects of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects whose nature admits poetic treatment; abstract technical or metaphysical material may demand attention and exposition counter to poetic aims. Anti-pattern: treating dense metaphysical argument as if it were lyrical subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_repetition_of_identical_faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated occurrence of the same stylistic fault across a work indicates a structural problem and warrants correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge’s schoolmaster tore up exercises when two identical faults appeared; similarly, works should be revised when the same flaw recurs. Scoring: recurring faults reduce overall quality more than isolated lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: truth_and_nativeness_of_thought_and_diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer truth and nativeness of thought and diction (a native, honest expression) over artificial elegance or foreign mannerisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge contrasts chaster, native diction (Catullus, Homer, elder English poets) with artificial fashions derived from Latin exercises and translation habits. Reward idiomatic, sincere expression; penalize learned-constructed lines that feel borrowed.
